title: DNS
concept: The Domain Name System maps human-readable names to the addresses machines route on. It is a hierarchical, distributed database: resolvers walk from the root to top-level domains to authoritative servers, and caching at every layer, bounded by each record's TTL, keeps the system fast at the cost of propagation delay.

points: DNS maps human-readable names to addresses through a hierarchy: resolvers walk from the root to top-level domains to authoritative servers.
Caching at every layer, bounded by each record's TTL, keeps it fast at the cost of propagation delay.
Cloudflare found that a design sized for yesterday's load becomes the bottleneck as traffic grows, so most changes now rebuild one record, not the whole zone.
Slack's DNSSEC rollout showed that an undo is just another change, and it spreads no faster than the longest cache in the path.

figures.label: 150x average speedup of per-record builds over full zone builds
less than 1% of Slack's online user base was affected by the DNSSEC outage

posts.title: How we improved DNS record build speed by more than 4,000x

digest.problem: When a customer edits a DNS record, the change has to reach Cloudflare's edge before queries return it. The slowest step was the Zone Builder, which reacted to any edit by rebuilding the whole zone: it read every record from the database, compared all of them against Quicksilver, Cloudflare's distributed key-value store, and fixed the differences. For very large zones that took tens of seconds per edit, and the rebuilds tied up database and Quicksilver capacity that other zones needed.
digest.constraints: Record changes had grown about 25-fold since the Zone Builder was written, and some zones hold millions of records. The database events that triggered builds did not say which record changed. Some zone settings, such as nameserver and DNSSEC controls, really do depend on the whole zone, so full builds could not simply be deleted. Millions of domains sit on this component, so the change had to be safe. The post also says per-record builds would not be possible without Cloudflare's "black lie" approach to negative answers with DNSSEC, because the normal approach needs every record in the zone sorted.

walkthrough.explanation: The database functions were changed so each record-level event carries the details of the record that was edited, instead of just naming the zone.
Those events go onto a new Kafka stream that the Zone Builder consumes.
The Zone Builder was split into scheduler types behind one interface: the old full-zone scheduler and a new per-record scheduler.

walkthrough.step: Apply one record at a time
walkthrough.explanation: The per-record scheduler takes events one by one, in order, and reads only the record that changed.
A dedicated Quicksilver interface writes the single change, and Quicksilver propagates it to the edge.
The schedulers lock against each other, so a slow full rebuild can never overwrite a newer per-record change with stale data.

walkthrough.step: Model updates as delete plus create
walkthrough.explanation: Update events were replaced by a deletion and a creation, so the old copy of a renamed record is cleaned up.

tradeoffs.chosen: Incremental per-record builds on a new event stream, with full rebuilds kept for zone-wide settings and a lock between the two.
tradeoffs.rejected: Rebuilding the whole zone on every edit, and later, sending record edits as single update events.
tradeoffs.why: Full rebuilds scale with zone size rather than with the size of the edit, and they burned shared database capacity. Per-record builds needed a new scheduling system and cannot be batched, but the post shows their advantage over full builds growing as zones get larger.

digest.failures: The first version sent update events containing only the new record. When a customer renamed a record, the old name was never removed from Quicksilver. The fix was to replace those update events with a creation event and a deletion event. Removing full builds entirely is still unfinished.
digest.takeaways: A design sized for yesterday's load becomes the bottleneck as traffic grows, so look for places where a small change triggers a large amount of work. Any incremental path needs protection from the old bulk path writing stale data over it. When a bug appears, change the design so that class of bug cannot happen again.

posts.title: The Case of the Recursive Resolvers (What Happened During Slack’s DNSSEC Rollout)

digest.problem: Slack had to sign its domains with DNSSEC to meet the FedRAMP Moderate compliance standard. On the third attempt to sign slack.com, some users could no longer resolve Slack's addresses and saw ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED, mostly behind Google Public DNS and certain corporate resolvers. Fewer than 1% of online users were affected, but the outage lasted 24 hours, and Slack's own rollback made part of it worse. It is an incident write-up, and it is here because it shows how DNS caching decides how fast any change, including an undo, can take effect.
digest.constraints: Route 53 served Slack's public zones, with some subzones delegated to NS1. DNSSEC can only be switched on for a whole domain, not one subdomain at a time, so every attempt risked all of slack.com. Resolvers differ in how strictly they apply the rules once signing is on. Most importantly, the DS record that links the .com zone to slack.com is cached for as long as the .com zone says, 24 hours, not for as long as Slack would like.

walkthrough.explanation: The team spent four months on DNSSEC, and other critical domains ran signed for at least a month before slack.com, all without trouble.
On September 7 they signed slack.com but rolled back early, as a precaution, while an unrelated outage at a large US ISP was generating reports.
On September 8 users on VPNs failed to resolve names, because some strict resolvers reject a CNAME at a zone's apex once the zone is signed. Slack switched those records to ALIAS records.

On September 30 they signed the zones, validated them with external monitors and debugging tools, waited three hours, and only then published the DS record at the registrar to complete the chain of trust.
When reports arrived, they removed the DS record to stop the damage, expecting resolvers to stop validating. Resolvers kept their cached copy for up to 24 hours.
After nearly an hour with no improvement they removed signing too. Resolvers still holding the cached DS record now expected signatures that no longer existed, and returned SERVFAIL for slack.com.
Slack asked ISPs and public resolver operators to flush slack.com and used public purge tools where offered. Errors fell as caches cleared, with a long tail until the cached DS record expired.

Network logs from Slack's client apps showed slack.com resolving while app.slack.com failed, which pointed at the wildcard record. Route 53 returned signed 'no such record' (NSEC) answers for the wildcard that did not list the record types that did exist. A query for an IPv6 (AAAA) address, which Slack did not publish, was read by resolvers like Google's as 'nothing exists at this name', cached, and then used to refuse ordinary lookups.

tradeoffs.chosen: A staged rollout: smaller domains first, then signing, validation and a soak period before publishing the DS record last. In the incident Slack pulled the DS record, then removed signing, which made things much worse, and then asked resolver operators to flush caches.
tradeoffs.rejected: Re-signing slack.com mid-incident, which would have used a different zone signing key, so validating resolvers would have kept failing, and signing subdomains one at a time, which DNSSEC does not allow.
tradeoffs.why: Publishing the DS record last should have made the change reversible, but that only holds if the DS record is not cached. Once resolvers had cached it, every rollback step had to wait for their caches, which Slack did not control.

digest.failures: Slack had never tested DNSSEC on a domain with a wildcard record before slack.com, and the wildcard is where Route 53's incomplete NSEC answers broke resolution. The team believed DS records were not cached, when the .com zone asked for 24 hours. Managing DNS through Terraform hid a warning that the Route 53 console shows when disabling DNSSEC, and the rollback deleted keys, one of which, the zone signing key, Route 53 would have regenerated differently. Route 53 has since fixed the NSEC bug.
digest.takeaways: In DNS, an undo is just another change, and it propagates no faster than the longest cache in the path, including caches set by a parent zone you do not own. Test on a domain shaped like your most important one, wildcards included. Read tool warnings during rollbacks, and use real client evidence, here network logs from Slack's clients, because resolvers that all follow the spec can still behave differently.

glossary.definition: The set of DNS records one operator is responsible for, usually a domain and its subdomains.
One entry in a zone, such as an A record mapping a name to an IPv4 address.
The server that holds the real answer for a zone, as opposed to a cache of it.
The server that looks up names on a client's behalf and caches the answers.
Time to live: how long a resolver may cache an answer before asking again.
The time between changing a record and every server answering with the new value.
Signatures on DNS answers that let a resolver check they came from the zone's owner and were not altered.
A record in the parent zone (such as .com) that vouches for a child zone's signing key, linking the two in a chain of trust.
The answer a resolver gives when it cannot produce a trustworthy response, for example when signatures it expects are missing.

mistakes: Expecting a DNS change to apply instantly. Resolvers may keep serving the old answer until its TTL expires, and the provider's own pipeline adds time on top.
Setting very long TTLs on records you may need to change quickly, such as before a migration. Lower the TTL well before the change, then raise it again.
Treating DNS as a load balancer. It can hand out several addresses, but cached answers mean it cannot react quickly when one server fails or gets overloaded.
comparison:
Both posts are about how long a DNS change takes to take effect, seen from opposite ends.

Cloudflare controlled the slow part, its own pipeline from a customer's edit to its edge, so it rebuilt that pipeline to apply one record in milliseconds instead of rebuilding a zone in tens of seconds.

Slack's slow part was outside its control: resolvers across the internet held its DS record for up to 24 hours and read its signed answers in different ways, so even its rollback could not take effect faster than those caches expired.

why.outcome: After this you can explain what problem DNS solves and why it has to be fast.
why.body:
Machines reach each other by IP address, but people and programs use names, and the address behind a name changes whenever a service moves. Something has to turn a name into an address before almost every connection starts.

Because that lookup sits in front of nearly everything, it has to be fast and it has to keep working when parts of the internet fail. That is why DNS is not one big directory: it is split across many servers, each responsible for its own part of the name space, with answers copied and cached all along the way.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture where an answer comes from and where copies of it are kept.
mentalModel.body:
Think of DNS as a chain of referrals with a cache at every step. Your device asks a recursive resolver. If the resolver has no copy, it asks a root server, which refers it to the servers for the top-level domain, such as .com, which refer it to the servers that are authoritative for the domain itself. Those give the real answer.

Every answer carries a TTL, a time to live that says how long anyone may reuse it. The authoritative servers hold the truth; everyone else holds copies that can be up to one TTL old. A change is therefore never seen everywhere at once: it spreads as old copies expire.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through a lookup step by step and say which steps a cache can skip.

steps.explanation: The device and the resolver first look for an unexpired copy of the answer. Most lookups end here.
On a miss, the resolver asks a root server, which does not know the answer but names the servers for the top-level domain.
The .com servers name the domain's authoritative servers. For a signed domain they also return a DS record that vouches for the domain's signing key.
They return the record, for example an address, along with its TTL. If the domain is signed, the resolver checks the signature against the DS record.
The resolver keeps each answer, including the referrals and DS record, for its TTL, and hands the address back to the device.
The owner edits the record at the authoritative servers. Each cache keeps serving its old copy until that copy's TTL runs out, so the change spreads gradually.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can trace a real lookup and predict how long a change, or an undo, takes to be seen.

steps.explanation: A browser asks its resolver, say Google Public DNS. With no copy cached, the resolver walks root, then .com.
Because Slack signed slack.com, .com returns a DS record along with the referral. The .com zone asks resolvers to keep it for 24 hours; Google's resolver caps that at 6 hours.
Route 53, which served Slack's zones, returns signed records. The resolver checks them against the cached DS record and caches the answer.
In Slack's incident the team pulled the DS record at the registrar. Resolvers that already had it cached kept expecting signatures for up to 24 hours, 6 on Google's resolver.
When Slack then removed signing, those resolvers could no longer validate any answer and returned SERVFAIL until their cached DS record expired.
In Cloudflare's one-million-record test zone, a per-record build took 8 ms or less, against about 34 seconds for a full build. After that, caches still serve the old copy until its TTL expires.

The time until everyone sees a change is roughly the provider's pipeline plus the longest TTL on any record in the path, and records cached at the parent zone, like the DS record, can hold on much longer than the record you changed.

quiz.question: A resolver has cached a record for example.com. You change the record at the authoritative servers. When does that resolver return the new value?
options: When its cached copy's TTL runs out and it asks again
Immediately, because the authoritative servers notify it
Only after you flush every resolver by hand
quiz.why: A resolver reuses its copy until the TTL expires, then asks again and gets the new value.
wrong: Authoritative servers do not notify resolvers of changes; resolvers only find out when they ask again.
Expiry makes the resolver ask again on its own; flushing only speeds it up.

quiz.question: Which servers hold the real answer for app.example.com?
options: Your recursive resolver, which stores the real records for every site you visit
The servers that are authoritative for example.com
The root servers, which hold the full record set for every top-level domain
The .com servers, which store each registered domain's records themselves
quiz.why: The authoritative servers for a domain hold its records; everyone else holds referrals or cached copies.
wrong: The resolver holds cached copies, which can be up to one TTL old.
Root servers only refer the resolver to the top-level domain servers.
The .com servers only refer the resolver to example.com's servers.

quiz.question: Why does DNS cache answers at every step?
options: So most lookups are answered nearby instead of walking the whole chain
quiz.why: Nearly every connection starts with a lookup, so reusing copies keeps lookups fast and keeps load off the servers higher up the chain.
wrong: Records do change, which is exactly why every answer carries a TTL.
Caching does not encrypt anything; DNSSEC signs answers so they can be checked, which is a separate thing.

quiz.question: On a cache miss, what does the .com server give a resolver looking up example.com?
options: The address of example.com, since the .com servers store every domain's records
Nothing; resolvers skip the .com servers and ask the root servers a second time
A referral to the servers that are authoritative for example.com
quiz.why: The top-level domain servers do not hold example.com's records. They point the resolver to the domain's authoritative servers, and for a signed domain also return a DS record.
wrong: Only the authoritative servers hold the record itself; .com only knows who they are.
On a miss the resolver has to ask .com to find out which servers are authoritative for the domain.

quiz.question: Slack pulled its DS record to stop an outage, but failures went on. Why?
options: Resolvers had cached the DS record, which .com tells them to keep for 24 hours
quiz.why: Removing the record at the parent does not reach resolvers that already cached it; they keep it until it expires.
wrong: The DS record was removed; the problem was copies already cached elsewhere.
DS records are checked by resolvers, not browsers.

quiz.question: You plan to move a site to a new address next week. What should you do with the record's TTL?
options: Raise it, so the new address sticks in caches before you switch over
Lower it well before the move, then raise it again afterwards
Nothing; TTLs do not affect moves because caches check the address every time
quiz.why: A short TTL before the move means caches drop the old address quickly once you switch; raising it afterwards restores caching.
wrong: A longer TTL makes caches keep the old address longer after you switch.
The TTL decides how long caches keep serving the old address, so it matters most during a move.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how two companies dealt with how long DNS changes take, from opposite ends.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain which part of a DNS change you control and which you do not.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply the concept to a change, design a pipeline, and plan for ten times the scale.

exercises.prompt: You must move api.example.com to a new address tomorrow, and its record has a long TTL. Plan the change so users switch quickly.
exercises.answer: Lower the TTL now, at least one old TTL before the move, so every cache has picked up the short value by the time you switch. Change the address, keep the old server running until the short TTL has passed, then raise the TTL again.
exercises.tradeoffs: A short TTL sends more queries to your authoritative servers while it is in place, and keeping the old server up costs a little extra.
wrongAnswers: Changing the address and expecting everyone to switch at once.
Lowering the TTL at the same moment as the move, while caches still hold the long one.
Turning off the old server right after the change.

exercises.prompt: Design how a DNS provider applies one customer's record edit so it reaches its servers quickly, even in zones with millions of records.
exercises.answer: Emit an event per changed record that carries the record itself, apply events per zone in order, and write only that record to the store the edge servers read. Keep a full rebuild for settings that depend on the whole zone, lock it against the per-record path so it never writes stale data over a newer edit, and send renames as a delete plus a create.
exercises.tradeoffs: More moving parts, a second build path to keep correct, and edits that cannot be batched, in exchange for a cost that stays flat as zones grow.
wrongAnswers: Rebuilding the whole zone for every edit.
Sending only the new value of an edited record, which leaves the old name behind after a rename.
Letting full rebuilds and per-record writes run without a lock.

exercises.prompt: Your main domain now carries ten times the traffic and has to be signed with DNSSEC. It has many subdomains, including a wildcard. Plan the rollout and the way back.
exercises.answer: Test signing on a domain shaped like the main one, wildcard included, and watch several public resolvers. Sign, validate, wait, and publish the DS record last. Plan the rollback around the parent's DS TTL: once published, removing the DS record does not take effect until cached copies expire, so keep signing in place and never delete keys until those caches have cleared.
exercises.tradeoffs: A slower rollout and more testing, against an outage that cannot be undone faster than other people's caches expire.
wrongAnswers: Assuming DS records are not cached.
Removing signing straight after pulling the DS record.
Testing only on simple domains without wildcards.

next.body: DNS can hand out several addresses for a name, but cached answers mean it cannot react quickly when one server is overloaded or down. Load Balancing picks up from there: making a fresh choice for every connection or request, close to the traffic.
